newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. town plans to form utility despite LILCO deal.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. town plans to form utility despite LILCO deal.

text.p: The village of Lynbrook on Long Island, N.Y., will stick to its plan to form its own utility despite a Brooklyn Union Gas and Long Island Lighting Co deal that would slash electric rates for LILCO customers by about 20 percent.
Late Tuesday, a town referendum won with 10 votes the support for Lynbrook to break away from LILCO, creating its own power company to serve its 19,500 residents.

Under the municipalization plan, Lynbrook residents could see their rate dropping to 8.75 cents a kilowatt-hour (KWh) from the current 17 cents/KWh, the highest in the country, while its commercial customers could see rate falling to 14 cents/KWh from the current LILCO rate of 32 cents/KWh.
Brooklyn Union and LILCO today agreed to a state takeover of LILCO's nuclear and regulatory assets, and electric transmission and distribution system for $1.7-1.9 billion.
The New York utilities announced their intention to merge on Dec 29, 1996, creating a $4 billion power and gas company.
Scarpato said Tuesday's vote gives Lynbrook the legal right to solicit bids to supply its annual energy need of 35 megawatts from brokers, marketers and other providers.
The village is already entertaining an unsolicited offer below 4 cents/KWh, he added.
It still needs to buy power poles and distribution lines from LILCO to bring outside generation into its territory. Those assets are valued between $15-17 million, Scarpato said.
But Lynbrook and LILCO are currently deadlocked on the proper fee for the village to leave LILCO's system.
"LILCO will treat things the same. They will not give things away," said Penelope Adelmann, analyst at Gruntal & Co.
The town estimates that exit cost at $20 million but LILCO assessed Lynbrook must pay $90 million for its distribution equipments and share of the Shoreham nuclear debacle.
Scarpato said the town has requested the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to decide on the proper amount it must pay LILCO to leave its system.
If FERC rules that Lynbrook must pay at least $80 million to LILCO, it would not be economic for the village to form its own power company, he said.
In addition to the exit fee, the town must consider the investment cost to form its own utility, analysts said.
"In the 8.75 cents/KWh rate, we figured in the startup costs," Scarpato said.
He estimates it would take $2 million to startup its own utility, which includes hiring support and operation employees and buying repair equipments.

"The reality is we believe that Lynbrook customers will pay significantly higher rates by having the village own and operate its own electric system than if they would remain with LILCO's or LIPA's system," said a LILCO spokeswoman.
